topics.title: Types, variables and operators
topics.objective: Understand primitive/reference types, conversions, expressions and operator edge cases.

concepts.title: Primitive values and references
concepts.objective: Distinguish copied primitive values from shared object references and understand char values.

cards.explanation: Primitive assignment copies the value. Updating copy does not update original; the alternatives treat the variables as aliases or ignore the assignment.
Both reference variables point to the same Box. Assignment does not clone the object, so changing its field is visible through both references.
char is an unsigned 16-bit integral type. Narrowing keeps the low 16 bits of -1, which represent 65535; it is neither signed short nor unsigned byte.

verification.code:
char value = (char) -1;
System.out.print((int) value);

concepts.title: Literals and local type inference
concepts.objective: Choose valid numeric literal forms and understand that var infers a fixed static type.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the unsuffixed integer literal is too large.
distractors: It prints 3000000000 after widening the literal to long.
It prints -1294967296 after wrapping the literal as int.
It throws ArithmeticException when the literal is assigned.
cards.explanation: A decimal integer literal without L must fit int. A long destination does not change the literal type; use 3_000_000_000L. The error precedes assignment.

verification.code:
long total = 3_000_000_000;
System.out.print(total);

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: number is int and cannot accept this double.
distractors: It prints 1.5 because var changes type on reassignment.
It prints 1 because assignment silently narrows the double.
It prints 1.5 because var always infers numeric values as double.
cards.explanation: var infers int from the initial literal and does not make the variable dynamically typed. Reassignment cannot perform an implicit double-to-int narrowing conversion.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: null alone cannot supply the inferred type.
distractors: It prints null because var infers Object from a null initializer.
It prints null because var declares a variable of the null type.
It throws NullPointerException while inferring the initializer type.
cards.explanation: A var declaration cannot infer its type from null alone. Declare a reference type explicitly, such as Object value = null; no runtime inference occurs.

verification.code:
var value = null;
System.out.print(value);

concepts.title: Initialization and definite assignment
concepts.objective: Distinguish default-initialized fields from local variables that must be assigned on every reachable path.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the local variable may be uninitialized.
distractors: It prints 0 because all int variables receive a default value.
It prints an unspecified value left in the local stack slot.
It throws NullPointerException when count is read.
cards.explanation: Local variables must be definitely assigned before use. Default initialization applies to fields and array elements, not local variables; Java does not expose an uninitialized stack value.

verification.code:
int count;
System.out.print(count);

cards.explanation: Instance fields have defaults: zero for int, false for boolean and null for references. A String field is not initialized to an empty string.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the false branch leaves score unassigned.
distractors: It prints 0 when args is empty because score gets a default.
It prints 10 even when args is empty because the assignment is checked.
It compiles, then throws an exception only when args is empty.
cards.explanation: The compiler cannot assume args.length is positive. There is a reachable path without assignment, so reading score fails definite-assignment analysis; this is not deferred to runtime.

concepts.title: Numeric promotion and narrowing assignments
concepts.objective: Predict promoted arithmetic types, constant-expression narrowing and compound-assignment conversions.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: adding these byte variables produces int.
distractors: It prints 30 because adding two bytes always produces byte.
It prints 30 because the compiler narrows any in-range result.
It throws ArithmeticException because byte arithmetic is forbidden.
cards.explanation: Binary numeric promotion converts these byte operands to int. Their sum is not a constant expression, and assignment cannot implicitly narrow the result merely because its runtime value fits.
Compound assignment includes conversion back to the left-hand type. The int result 128 narrows to byte -128; Java does not throw on this integer overflow.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: 128 is outside the byte assignment range.
distractors: It prints 127 -128 because every int literal silently narrows.
It prints 127 128 because byte widens to hold this initializer.
It throws ArithmeticException while assigning high.
cards.explanation: An int constant expression may narrow in assignment only when its value fits the destination type. 127 fits byte; 128 does not. An explicit cast would be a different program.

concepts.title: Integer overflow, division and remainder
concepts.objective: Identify arithmetic overflow before widening and predict division/remainder for negative integers.

cards.explanation: int addition wraps when the mathematical result is outside its signed 32-bit range. It does not saturate, automatically widen or throw ArithmeticException.

verification.code:
int value = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
System.out.print(value + 1);

cards.explanation: Both operands are int, so multiplication overflows before assignment widens the result to long. Use 50_000L * 50_000 to calculate in long arithmetic.

verification.code:
long result = 50_000 * 50_000;
System.out.print(result);

cards.question:
Java 27: What happens when this code is used inside main?

```java
System.out.print((-7 / 3) + " " + (-7 % 3));
```
cards.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero. The remainder satisfies dividend = quotient * divisor + remainder and has the dividend sign when nonzero. These rules give -2 and -1.

verification.code: System.out.print((-7 / 3) + " " + (-7 % 3));

concepts.title: Floating-point special values and precision
concepts.objective: Recognize NaN, infinity and limits of binary floating-point equality.

cards.explanation: Floating-point zero divided by zero produces NaN. NaN is unequal even to itself. Unlike integer division by zero, this floating-point operation does not throw ArithmeticException.

verification.code:
double value = 0.0 / 0.0;
System.out.print(value == value);

cards.explanation: A positive finite nonzero double divided by positive zero gives positive infinity. Zero divided by zero instead gives NaN; integer divide-by-zero exception rules do not apply.

verification.code:
double value = 1.0 / 0.0;
System.out.print(value);

cards.question:
Java 27: What happens when this code is used inside main?

```java
System.out.print((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3);
```
cards.explanation: These decimal fractions are approximated in binary floating point; the rounded sum differs from the representation of 0.3. Use a suitable tolerance or decimal arithmetic when the domain requires it.

verification.code: System.out.print((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3);

concepts.title: Equality, boxing and null unboxing
concepts.objective: Distinguish value comparisons from reference identity and detect null unboxing.

cards.explanation: The other operand is primitive int, so value is unboxed and numeric equality compares 1000 with 1000. This does not compare two boxed references or depend on an Integer cache.

verification.code:
Integer value = 1000;
System.out.print(value == 1000);

distractors: It prints the reference value null.
It fails because Integer cannot hold null.
cards.explanation: Integer is a reference type and can hold null. Assigning it to int requires unboxing, which throws for null; no primitive default substitutes for the missing object.
The two new expressions create distinct objects, so reference identity is false. String.equals compares their equal contents. Reference identity and value equality are separate operations.

concepts.title: Evaluation order and short-circuit operators
concepts.objective: Predict left-to-right side effects, skipped boolean operands and string concatenation.

cards.explanation: The left operand is evaluated first. Post-increment contributes 2 then sets value to 3; pre-increment sets it to 4 before contributing its value.

verification.code:
int value = 2;
System.out.print(value++ + " " + ++value);

cards.explanation: When the left operand of && is false, Java skips the right operand. count is therefore not incremented and the result is false. Single & would evaluate both operands.

cards.question:
Java 27: What happens when this code is used inside main?

```java
System.out.print("sum=" + 1 + 2);
```
cards.explanation: The additions associate left to right. Once a String is involved, + concatenates: sum= plus 1, then plus 2. Parenthesize 1 + 2 to obtain numeric addition first.

verification.code: System.out.print("sum=" + 1 + 2);

topics.title: Control flow
topics.objective: Reason about branches, loops, switch expressions and execution order.

concepts.title: Boolean conditions and branch binding
concepts.objective: Require boolean conditions, detect unboxing in branches and understand which if owns an else.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the assignment expression has type int.
distractors: It prints yes because assigning 1 makes the condition truthy.
It prints no because assignment expressions are always false.
It compiles but throws because assignments are forbidden at runtime.
cards.explanation: Java if conditions require boolean or Boolean. Assigning 1 to an int produces an int, not a truth value; this is not the score == 1 comparison.
Without braces, the else belongs to the nearest eligible if: if (inner). outer is true, inner is false, so its else prints B; indentation does not change binding.

distractors: It prints no because null means false.
It prints yes because the reference exists.
It fails because Boolean is not a condition type.
cards.explanation: Boolean is allowed as a condition but must be unboxed. A null reference throws before either branch runs; null does not act as a false primitive boolean.

concepts.title: For-loop boundaries and empty bodies
concepts.objective: Count iterations accurately and distinguish a loop body from a trailing empty statement.

cards.explanation: The body runs for i = 0, 1 and 2. The exclusive upper bound excludes 3, and the sum is 3; counting iterations is not the same as summing the index.
The inclusive bound includes i = 3, so the body adds 1 + 2 + 3. Omitting the final iteration or including 4 gives the incorrect alternatives.
The semicolon is the entire empty loop body. The loop still increments i until its condition fails at 3; the following print is executed once outside the loop.

concepts.title: While and do-while evaluation
concepts.objective: Distinguish pre-tested/post-tested loops and include side effects from the final failed test.

cards.explanation: while checks the condition before the body. count < 0 is initially false, so the increment never runs; a loop does not guarantee one iteration.
do-while executes its body before checking the condition. The increment runs once, then 1 < 0 is false; it differs from the corresponding while loop.
The comparison uses the old value and then increments i. Tests with old values 0 and 1 pass; the final test with old value 2 fails but still increments i to 3.

concepts.title: Break, continue and for-loop updates
concepts.objective: Distinguish exiting a loop from skipping its current body and understand for updates after continue.

cards.explanation: continue skips only the rest of the current iteration. The loop still visits 3 and 4, adding 1 + 3 + 4; it neither adds 2 nor exits the loop.
break exits the loop when i is 3, before that value is added. Only 1 and 2 contribute; it does not merely skip the third iteration.
A continue targeting a basic for loop proceeds to its update expressions. i advances past 1, so the loop terminates at 3 and visits is incremented for 0 and 2 only.

concepts.title: Nested loops and labeled transfers
concepts.objective: Identify the loop targeted by unlabeled/labeled break and continue without skipping or inventing iterations.

cards.explanation: break outer exits the labeled outer loop immediately after the first increment. An unlabeled break would exit only the inner loop and allow later outer iterations.
The unlabeled break targets the inner loop. Each of the three outer iterations increments visits at j = 0, then breaks at j = 1; the outer loop continues.
continue outer ends the current outer iteration when j = 1 and executes the outer for update. Each outer iteration therefore increments visits only at j = 0.

concepts.title: Colon switch groups and fall-through
concepts.objective: Trace colon-style case groups, missing matches and null selectors.

cards.explanation: Execution begins at matching case 2 and falls through into case 3. Its break prevents default from running; earlier case 1 is not revisited.

This ordinary int switch statement may omit default. With no matching case, none of its body runs and execution continues after the switch. Switch expressions have different exhaustiveness requirements.

distractors: It prints other via the default case.
It prints go after converting null to text.
It fails because String selectors are unsupported.
cards.explanation: A null String selector is not handled by default. With no explicit case null, selection throws NullPointerException; String selectors themselves are supported.

concepts.title: Arrow switch rules, yield and exhaustiveness
concepts.objective: Predict non-falling-through arrow rules and return values from exhaustive switch expressions.

cards.explanation: An arrow rule supplies its value without falling through into later rules. The matching rule yields two; no break statement is necessary.
yield supplies the value of the enclosing switch expression. The local value is 20 and the yielded expression is value * 2; yield is not a method return.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the switch expression is not exhaustive.
distractors: It prints 10 because selector currently contains 1.
It prints 0 because unmatched values receive an implicit default.
It throws only if selector contains a value other than 1.
cards.explanation: A switch expression must cover all possible selector values. A non-final int variable initialized to 1 does not limit its static domain; add a default rule for this int expression.

verification.expected: does not cover all possible input values

concepts.title: Scope and statement reachability
concepts.objective: Respect for-variable scope and distinguish Java reachability rules for while and if.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: i is outside its declared scope.
distractors: It prints 2 because the loop variable survives afterward.
It prints 1 because the final body iteration used that value.
It prints 0 because the loop variable is reinitialized afterward.
cards.explanation: The for initializer variable is scoped to the loop, including its condition/update/body. It cannot be named after the loop; declare it outside when its final value is needed.

verification.code:
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { }
System.out.print(i);

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the while body is unreachable.
distractors: It prints done because every false branch is allowed.
It prints neverdone because the body runs before its test.
It prints nothing because the loop prevents later execution.
cards.explanation: A while with constant false has an unreachable body, which Java rejects. This differs from the special reachability rules allowing if (false) bodies and from post-tested do-while.

verification.code:
while (false) { System.out.print("never"); }
System.out.print("done");

cards.explanation: Java permits an if (false) body under its special reachability rules, supporting conditional compilation patterns. The branch is not executed, and the later print runs normally.

verification.code:
if (false) { System.out.print("never"); }
System.out.print("done");
